title: Database Indexing
sources: Use The Index, Luke (use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy/the-tree): a database index is a B-tree whose depth grows logarithmically, so even millions of entries need only a few levels; a lookup walks root to leaf in a few steps
Use The Index, Luke (use-the-index-luke.com/sql/dml/insert): every index on a table must be updated on each insert, so more indexes make writes slower

DesignGurus 'Database indexing' and roadmap.sh 'How database indexes work': without an index the database does a full table scan reading every row; an index is a sorted structure, like a book's index, pointing to where each row lives
AlgoMaster 'The hidden cost of database indexes': indexes use extra storage and slow INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, so index the columns you actually query

lines.text: Yesterday we saved every pizza order,
but now there are ten million of them,
and a customer calls asking about Ravi's order.
Without help, the database checks every row,
one by one, like flipping through every page of a book.
lines.caps: ONE BY *ONE | LIKE *FLIPPING | THROUGH EVERY *PAGE | OF A *BOOK

lines.text: It's like the index at the back of a textbook,
lines.caps: IT'S *LIKE | THE *INDEX | AT THE *BACK | OF A *TEXTBOOK

lines.text: each pointing to exactly where its row lives.
Databases keep it as a tree,
so even ten million rows take just a few hops.
lines.caps: SO *EVEN | TEN MILLION *ROWS | TAKE *JUST | A FEW *HOPS

lines.text: Every new order has to update the index too,
lines.caps: EVERY NEW *ORDER | HAS TO *UPDATE | THE INDEX *TOO

lines.text: Index what you search, not everything.
